In [[mathematics]], the '''Schneider–Lang theorem''' is a refinement by {{harvtxt| Lang|1966}} of a theorem of {{harvtxt|Schneider|1949}} about the [[transcendental number|transcendence]] of values of [[meromorphic function]]s.  The theorem implies both the [[Hermite–Lindemann theorem|Hermite–Lindemann]] and [[Gelfond–Schneider theorem]]s, and implies the transcendence of some values of [[elliptic function]]s and [[elliptic modular function]]s.

== Statement ==
Fix a [[number field]] {{mvar|K}} and [[meromorphic]] {{math|''f''<sub>1</sub>, ..., ''f''<sub>''N''</sub>}}, of which at least two are algebraically independent and have [[entire function|order]]s {{math|''ρ''<sub>1</sub>}} and {{math|''ρ''<sub>2</sub>}}, and such that {{math|''f{{sub|j}}{{prime}}'' &isin; ''K''[''f''{{sub|1}}, ..., ''f''{{sub|''N''}}]}} for any {{mvar|j}}.  Then there are at most 
: <math>(\rho_1+\rho_2) [K:\mathbb{Q}] \,</math>
distinct [[complex number]]s {{math|''ω''<sub>1</sub>, ..., ''ω<sub>m</sub>''}} such that {{math|''f''<sub>''i''</sub>(''ω<sub>j</sub>'') &isin; ''K''}} for all combinations of {{mvar|i}} and {{mvar|j}}.  

== Examples ==

* If {{math|''f''<sub>1</sub>(''z'')&nbsp;{{=}}&nbsp;''z''}} and {{math|''f''<sub>2</sub>(''z'')&nbsp;{{=}}&nbsp;''e''<sup>''z''</sup>}} then the theorem implies the [[Hermite–Lindemann theorem]] that {{math|''e<sup>α</sup>''}} is transcendental for nonzero [[algebraic number|algebraic]] {{mvar|α}}: otherwise, {{math|''α'', 2''α'', 3''α'', ...}} would be an infinite number of values at which both {{math|''f''<sub>1</sub>}} and {{math|''f''<sub>2</sub>}} are algebraic.
* Similarly taking {{math|''f''<sub>1</sub>(''z'')&nbsp;{{=}}&nbsp;''e''<sup>''z''</sup>}} and {{math|''f''<sub>2</sub>(''z'')&nbsp;{{=}}&nbsp;''e''<sup>''βz''</sup>}} for {{mvar|β}} [[irrational number|irrational]] algebraic implies the [[Gelfond–Schneider theorem]] that if {{mvar|α}} and {{math|''α''<sup>''β''</sup>}} are algebraic, then {{math|α&nbsp;&isin; {0,1}}}: otherwise, {{math|log(''α''), 2log(''α''), 3log(''α''), ...}} would be an infinite number of values at which both  {{math|''f''<sub>1</sub>}} and  {{math|''f''<sub>2</sub>}} are algebraic.
* Recall that the [[Weierstrass P function]] satisfies the [[differential equation]]
:: <math> \wp'(z)^2 = 4\wp(z)^3-g_2\wp(z)-g_3. \,</math>
: Taking the three functions to be {{math|''z''}}, {{math|℘(''αz'')}}, {{math|℘{{prime}}(''αz'')}} shows that, for any algebraic {{mvar|α}}, if {{math|''g''<sub>2</sub>(''α'')}} and {{math|''g''<sub>3</sub>(''α'')}} are algebraic, then {{math|℘(''α'')}} is transcendental.
* Taking the functions to be {{math|''z''}} and {{math|''e''<sup> ''f''(''z'')</sup>}} for a [[polynomial]] {{mvar|f}} of [[degree of a polynomial|degree]] {{mvar|ρ}} shows that the number of points where the functions are all algebraic can grow linearly with the order {{math|''ρ''&nbsp;{{=}}&nbsp;deg&nbsp;''f''}}.

== Proof ==

To [[mathematical proof|prove]] the result Lang took two algebraically independent functions from {{math|''f''<sub>1</sub>, ..., ''f''<sub>''N''</sub>}}, say, {{mvar|f}} and {{mvar|g}}, and then created an auxiliary function {{math|''F'' &isin; ''K''[ ''f'', ''g'']}}.  Using [[Siegel's lemma]], he then showed that one could assume {{mvar|F}} vanished to a high order at the {{math|ω<sub>1</sub>, ..., ω<sub>''m''</sub>}}.  Thus a high-order [[derivative]] of {{mvar|F}} takes a value of small size at one such {{math|ω<sub>''i''</sub>}}s, "size" here referring to [[Height function|an algebraic property of a number]].  Using the [[maximum modulus principle]], Lang also found a separate estimate for absolute values of derivatives of {{mvar|F}}.  Standard results connect the size of a number and its absolute value, and the combined estimates imply the claimed bound on {{mvar|m}}.

== Bombieri's theorem ==
{{harvtxt|Bombieri|Lang|1970}} and {{harvtxt|Bombieri|1970}} generalized the result to functions of several variables. Bombieri showed that if ''K'' is an algebraic number field and ''f''<sub>1</sub>,&nbsp;...,&nbsp;''f''<sub>''N''</sub> are meromorphic functions of ''d'' complex variables of order at most ρ generating a field ''K''(''f''<sub>1</sub>,&nbsp;...,&nbsp;''f''<sub>''N''</sub>) of transcendence degree at least ''d''&nbsp;+ 1 that is closed under all [[partial derivative]]s, then the set of points where all the functions ''f''<sub>''n''</sub> have values in ''K'' is contained in an algebraic hypersurface in '''C'''<sup>''d''</sup> of degree at most 
:<math>d((d+1)\rho[K:\mathbb{Q}]+1).</math>
{{harvtxt|Waldschmidt|1979|loc=theorem 5.1.1}} gave a simpler proof of Bombieri's theorem, with a slightly stronger bound of ''d''(ρ<sub>1</sub> + ... + ρ<sub>''d''+1</sub>)[''K'':'''Q'''] for the degree, where the ρ<sub>''j''</sub> are the orders of ''d''&nbsp;+ 1 algebraically independent functions.  The special case ''d''&nbsp;= 1 gives the Schneider&ndash;Lang theorem, with a bound of (ρ<sub>1</sub> + ρ<sub>2</sub>)[''K'':'''Q''']  for the number of points.

===Example===
If <math>p</math> is a polynomial with [[integer]] [[coefficient]]s then the functions <math>z_1,...,z_n,e^{p(z_1,...,z_n)}</math> are all algebraic at a dense set of points of the hypersurface <math>p=0</math>.
